name: Takar the Seer
summary: East of Camp Taurajo, Takar the Seer keeps a lone camp in the Barrens. Though surrounded by Horde lands, he remains loyal to the Alliance and shares occult knowledge with certain travelers.

sections.title: A Recluse in the Savannah
sections.body: Takar the Seer lives alone beneath a simple tent east of Camp Taurajo. Tauren braves and orc patrols watch the surrounding Barrens, yet leave his remote clearing undisturbed. He distrusts curious Horde visitors but rarely starts a fight, keeping watch on the horizon and to himself. His camp lies far from Stormwind's politics.

sections.title: Occult Counsel
sections.body: Takar the Seer shares his knowledge with a few visitors from beyond his camp. Alliance warlocks who come from the Eastern Kingdoms seek his cryptic counsel when they try to bind dangerous beings from beyond this world. His understanding of hidden forces and the craft of souls draws these practitioners to his remote, perilous camp.

faq.q: Why is a human seer living alone in the Barrens?
aliases: why is takar in the barrens
faq.answer: Takar has never said why he lives alone. His camp lies east of Camp Taurajo, far from any Alliance outpost, and warlocks visit for his knowledge of demons rather than his story.

faq.q: Is Takar hostile to Horde players?
faq.answer: Yes. Takar is aligned with the Alliance, so Horde adventurers find him hostile. He rarely attacks unless provoked or approached too closely.

faq.q: What brings Alliance adventurers to his camp?
faq.answer: Alliance seekers, especially warlocks, come to Takar for guidance in binding powerful demons such as the Succubus. He offers cryptic instructions and insight into the reagents needed to summon and dominate them.

angles.text: As an Alliance warlock, you can turn to Takar in Kalimdor for guidance through the dangerous rites that summon and bind a succubus to your service.
As an Alliance traveler, you can find a friendly human far within Horde territory, though Takar keeps to his solitary camp in central Kalimdor.
